description: A2AD dialectic review mode evidence examples covering full review, minimal review, cancellation, synthesis with dissenting notes, and fact/assumption/recommendation separation.

evidence.title: Design review: Workflow engine migration to state-machine model

data.title: Migrate workflow engine to state-machine model
data.summary: Replace the current callback-chain workflow engine with an explicit state-machine model for better observability, testability, and error recovery.
claims: State-machine model reduces unrecoverable failure rate
State-machine is easier to unit test than callback chains
Migration can be done incrementally per workflow type
assumptions: All current callback-chain workflows have a finite and enumerable state set
Migration per workflow type takes at most 2 weeks
The state-machine library supports all required transition guards
risksIdentified: Long-running workflows in callback state during migration may need dual-path support
State-machine library learning curve for the team
data.recommendation: Proceed with incremental migration, starting with the order-processing workflow as a pilot
testCriteria: Order-processing workflow passes 100% of existing E2E tests after migration
P99 latency does not increase by more than 5%
Error recovery rate improves by at least 30%

counterClaims: State-machine model adds ceremony without proportional benefit for simple workflows
Migration cost exceeds projected reliability gains for workflows nearing end-of-life
Incremental migration introduces dual-engine complexity in production
failureModes: Dual-engine runtime paths create unexpected interaction bugs
State-machine library API changes during migration window
Team productivity drops during the 12-week migration period
contradictions: The comparison benchmark only covers 3 of 12 workflow types
The callback-chain failure rate is already below 0.1% — reduction may not justify migration cost
assumptionsChallenged: Not all workflows have a clean finite state set — some have ad-hoc callback logic that does not map to discrete states
Two weeks per workflow type underestimates testing and validation time
risksRaised: Dual-engine cognitive load during migration period
Regressions in non-migrated workflows due to shared infrastructure changes

data.response: The critic raises valid concerns about dual-engine complexity and migration scope. However, the end-of-life concern is addressed by excluding EOL workflows from migration scope.
defendedClaims: State-machine model improves observability — current callback-chain lacks a single source of truth for workflow state
Incremental migration is feasible with feature flags per workflow type
concededPoints: Migration timeline estimate of 2 weeks per type is optimistic; revised to 3 weeks
Dual-engine complexity during migration needs a detailed coexistence plan
refinedAssumptions: Workflows with ad-hoc callback logic that cannot be cleanly state-mapped will be excluded from scope
Feature flags allow per-workflow-type rollout and instant rollback
residualRisks: Shared infrastructure changes during migration may still affect non-migrated workflows

preserved: Incremental migration with feature flags is feasible
Excluding EOL and ad-hoc workflows from scope reduces risk
rejected: All 12 workflow types must be migrated (revised scope: 8/12, exclude 4 EOL/ad-hoc)
Two weeks per workflow type (revised estimate: 3 weeks)
dissentingNotes: Critic noted that the callback-chain failure rate is already below 0.1%, and the improvement may not justify cost. Overruled because the observability and testability gaps are strategic quality investments, not purely failure-rate driven. This note is preserved for cost-benefit review after phase 1.
facts: Current workflow engine uses callback chains with no explicit state model
Order-processing workflow handles 40% of production traffic
Three of twelve workflow types are nearing end-of-life
Callback-chain unrecoverable failure rate is 0.08%
State-machine library v2.1 supports all required transition guards
assumptions: Feature flags suffice for coexistence (confidence: medium — needs production testing in phase 0)
3 weeks per workflow type with dedicated engineer (confidence: medium)
Order-processing workflow is representative of other target workflows (confidence: high)
risks: Dual-engine runtime interaction bugs (phase 0 pilot reduces this)
Team productivity drop during migration (mitigated by training session before phase 1)
State-machine library future API stability (low probability, high impact)
tests: Phase 0: order-processing workflow migration in staging with 7 days of production traffic replay
Phase 1 gate: P99 latency delta ≤ 5%, error recovery rate improves ≥ 30%
Phase 2 gate: 100% E2E pass rate on migrated workflows
data.recommendation: Proceed with incremental migration: phase 0 (order-processing pilot, 3 weeks), then phase 1-3 (7 remaining workflows, 3 weeks each) with go/no-go gate after each phase
data.recommendationBasis: The observability and testability benefits justify the migration cost for 8 of 12 workflow types. The phased approach with explicit gates and the order-processing pilot reduces risk. EOL and ad-hoc workflows are excluded.

facts: Current workflow engine uses callback chains with no explicit state model
Order-processing workflow handles 40% of production traffic
Three of twelve workflow types are nearing end-of-life
Callback-chain unrecoverable failure rate is 0.08%
State-machine library v2.1 supports all required transition guards
assumptions: Feature flags suffice for coexistence (confidence: medium)
3 weeks per workflow type with dedicated engineer (confidence: medium)
Order-processing workflow is representative (confidence: high)
tests: Phase 0: order-processing pilot in staging with traffic replay
Phase 1 gate: P99 latency delta ≤ 5%, error recovery rate improves ≥ 30%
Phase 2 gate: 100% E2E pass rate on migrated workflows
dissentingNotes: Critic noted callback-chain failure rate is already below 0.1%. Overruled because observability and testability are strategic quality investments.
synthesisCard.recommendation: Proceed with phased migration (8 of 12 workflow types), starting with order-processing pilot

evidence.title: Config change: Increase broker task timeout from 10m to 15m

data.title: Increase broker default task timeout to 15 minutes
data.summary: Heavy analysis tasks regularly exceed the 10-minute default timeout. A 15-minute default reduces failure retries without operator intervention.
claims: 15-minute timeout covers 95% of current heavy tasks
Operator overhead decreases by reducing manual timeout overrides
assumptions: No task should take more than 15 minutes under normal conditions
The broker can handle longer task leases without resource exhaustion
risksIdentified: Runaway tasks consume worker slots longer
data.recommendation: Increase default task timeout from 10 minutes to 15 minutes

counterClaims: Runaway task risk increases with longer timeout
95% coverage is not enough — the 5% outlier tasks should be individually configured, not by raising the default
failureModes: Worker pool exhaustion if multiple runaway tasks coincide
contradictions: The statistics document counts completed tasks only, not tasks that timed out at 10m and were retried with 15m — selection bias
assumptionsChallenged: Broker resource exhaustion bound is not quantified in the thesis
risksRaised: Worker slot starvation under concurrent heavy loads

preserved: Runaway task risk is real and needs a mitigation
rejected: Raising the default unconditionally (mitigated by adding a per-task cap)
dissentingNotes: Critic noted selection bias in the timeout statistics. Acknowledged — the 95% figure should be re-validated with uncensored data before making the change permanent.
facts: Heavy analysis tasks regularly exceed 10 minutes
The broker supports per-task timeout configuration
assumptions: Broker worker slot exhaustion can be monitored via existing dashboards (confidence: high)
risks: Runaway tasks consume worker slots longer — mitigated by adding a per-worker max runtime cap of 30 minutes
tests: Deploy change to staging and run 100 heavy analysis tasks; verify < 5% exceed 15m
data.recommendation: Increase default task timeout to 15 minutes and add a per-worker max runtime cap of 30 minutes. Re-validate the 95% coverage figure after 1 week.
data.recommendationBasis: The change is low-risk and revertible. The per-worker cap prevents runaway exhaustion. The 95% figure should be re-validated as a follow-up task, not a blocker.

facts: Heavy analysis tasks regularly exceed 10 minutes
Broker supports per-task timeout configuration
assumptions: Worker slot exhaustion is monitorable via existing dashboards (confidence: high)
risks: Runaway tasks consume slots longer — mitigated by 30-minute per-worker max cap
tests: Staging validation with 100 heavy analysis tasks
dissentingNotes: Selection bias in 95% figure — re-validate after 1 week
synthesisCard.recommendation: Increase default timeout to 15m with 30m per-worker cap; re-validate 95% coverage

evidence.title: Incident analysis: Database connection pool exhaustion on 2026-05-24

data.title: Root cause analysis: DB pool exhaustion
data.summary: A sudden spike in connection requests due to a misconfigured connection leak detector caused the pool to exhaust.
claims: Connection leak detector was deployed with overly aggressive thresholds
Rolling back the detector resolved the issue within 5 minutes
assumptions: The leak detector was correctly identified as the root cause
No ongoing connection leaks remain in the system
risksIdentified: Leak detector re-deployment needs better staging validation
data.recommendation: Increase pool size permanently and re-deploy leak detector with safe defaults

counterClaims: Pool size increase masks the underlying problem rather than fixing it
The leak detector may have revealed a real leak that needs investigation
failureModes: Increasing pool size delays detection of future actual leaks
contradictions: 5-minute recovery does not prove the detector was the root cause — correlation is not causation
assumptionsChallenged: No ongoing connection leak — this is unverified
risksRaised: Masking a real leak by increasing pool size could lead to a larger incident later

data.response: The critic's concern about masking is valid. However, increasing the pool size is a safety margin, not a fix. The leak detector re-deployment with safe defaults is the actual fix.
defendedClaims: The leak detector thresholds were incorrectly configured
concededPoints: A thorough leak investigation should precede leak detector re-deployment
Pool size increase alone is insufficient without root cause verification
refinedAssumptions: Leak investigation must confirm no real leak exists before re-deploying the detector
residualRisks: Incident may recur if a real leak exists and the detector was falsely triggering

preserved: Leak detector thresholds were aggressive — this contributed to the incident
Pool size increase is a safety margin, not a root cause fix
rejected: Leak detector was the sole root cause (unproven — correlation, not causation)
Pool size increase alone is sufficient mitigation
dissentingNotes: Critic argued that pool size increase masks real leaks. This concern has merit. The recommendation below requires a thorough leak investigation before re-deploying the detector. This dissenting note is preserved so the operator sees both positions.
facts: Connection pool was exhausted at 2026-05-24T14:23Z
Leak detector was deployed on 2026-05-23 with aggressive thresholds
Rolling back the detector freed connections within 5 minutes
No unexplained connection growth has been observed since rollback
assumptions: No real connection leak exists (confidence: medium — 24 hours of clean data is promising but not definitive)
Aggressive leak detector thresholds were the trigger, not a pre-existing leak (confidence: medium)
risks: A real leak may exist and was unmasked by the detector (low probability, high impact)
Increasing pool size without investigation masks future symptoms
tests: Leak investigation: instrument connection lifecycle and monitor for 7 days before re-deploying the detector
Pool size validation: verify no performance regression with increased pool under peak load
data.recommendation: Increase pool size by 50% as a safety margin. Before re-deploying the leak detector, run a 7-day connection lifecycle investigation to confirm no real leak exists. Re-deploy the detector with the verified safe thresholds only after investigation passes.
data.recommendationBasis: The immediate safety margin (pool increase) addresses current risk. The investigation (step 2) addresses the critic's valid concern about masking real leaks. The detector re-deployment (step 3) restores the intended monitoring capability.

facts: Connection pool exhausted at 2026-05-24T14:23Z
Leak detector deployed with aggressive thresholds
Rollback freed connections within 5 minutes
assumptions: No real leak exists (confidence: medium)
Aggressive thresholds were the trigger (confidence: medium)
risks: A real leak may exist — investigate before re-deploying detector
Pool size increase without investigation masks future symptoms
dissentingNotes: Critic: pool size increase masks real leaks. Recommendation requires investigation before re-deploying detector. Preserved so both positions are visible to operator.
synthesisCard.recommendation: Increase pool 50%; investigate for 7 days before re-deploying leak detector with safe thresholds
